rv.q: If 2025 sees a finer or more accomplished piece of playwriting, I will be very surprised.
Sheehy’s originality makes an evocative play unmissable.
Its haunting imagery will stay with you for a long time.

A year after her Olivier-nominated performance in Machinal, Sheehy’s transformative, vanity and cliche-free turn here underscores how damn good she is and hopefully permanently elevates her to leading-actor status.
The leaps the takes as a writer into the numinous here won’t be to everyone’s taste but I bloody loved it.
Although the piece is profoundly slow-moving, it remains gripping thanks to McPherson's typically sparkling dialogue, dripping with vibrant Irish idiom and loaded with humour and profundity.
Sometimes this production lifts off, as if it is about to enter into the sublime, but is strangely dragged down by too many elements jostling to take flight.
I’m not sure it quite adds up, but it’s far more interesting than plenty of plays that do.
Still, somehow the plot of The Brightening Air never takes a definitive shape.
There’s a joyous understatement in the colourful dabs of humour, tinged as they are with sadness and the profound regret for things either lost, or that never were.
The play is still brimming with more fantasy and good fun than most.
It’s a frustrating play, always watchable, so nearly great, so nearly soaring, yet somehow held earthbound by the weight of its intent.
I can't say I was as moved by The Brightening Air as I had hoped I might be, given McPherson's proven gift for the numinous...
That dog, like the play, is serviceable, but it’s not quite all you were hoping for.
It is a production that envelops you in the warmth and melancholy of rural Ireland, delivering a family drama that is as evocative as it is quietly magical.
Skipping over his adaptations, surely The Brightening Air redeems that bald self-proscription.

With Rae Smith’s ghostly yet grounded design, helped by Mark Henderson’s lighting and Gregory Clarke’s sound, which create a real feel of the uncanny, The Brightening Air is both elegiacally written and poetically resonant.
But beside the story at hand it is hard to say what the evening adds up to.

Unfortunately, there's hardly anything visually or narratively engaging about The Brightening Air, other than for Gregory Clarke's sound design and Ben McQuinn on associate music capturing a beautiful, gentle and fascinating ambience which is never really replicated in McPherson's writing and direction, making for a tiring slog of a show instead.
The Brightening Air fizzles at times with its own potential, but never truly bubbles over in this relaxed, sometimes-unfocused production.
The trouble is if the theme is inertia it needs a lot else to keep it interesting and I could never quite get my head round what The Brightening Air was actually trying to be.

cn.t: McPherson's first original play in 12 years divides critics with its slow-moving, Chekhov-inspired Irish family drama. While some praise the sparkling dialogue and mystical atmosphere, others find it mundane and overly derivative.

vr.q: Either way, it's great entertainment showcasing an outstanding cast.
I do have some serious question marks about its depictions of neurodivergent characters, but I also think it offers enough compelling character study to really make it worth seeing.
